docs.title: sfx-olly
docs.text:
A Python CLI and library for Splunk Observability Cloud: discover metrics, query their values with SignalFlow, inspect detectors/incidents, and receive alert webhooks.

Requires Python 3.10+ and an API-scoped token for querying your organization. Metric queries run once and exit; the webhook receiver stays running to accept notifications. Raw traces and logs are not currently supported.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
From the project checkout:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e .

Without the installed command, use python -m sfx_olly instead of sfx-olly.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
cp .env.example .env

Edit your local .env to set SFX_TOKEN and the correct SFX_REALM. Run commands from that directory; real environment variables override .env. Keep credentials out of source control and support messages.

See the configuration reference for timeouts, retries, corporate CA certificates, logging, and webhook settings.

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
All example metric names, projects, and environments below are fictional. Replace them with values discovered in your organization; these examples are not seeded data.

# Discover metric names and their dimensions.
sfx-olly metrics search 'example.*' --limit 20
sfx-olly metrics inspect example.project.size

# Read a project's values, without combining different series.
sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test --filter project.name=project-demo \
  --range 1h --resolution 1m --unit kib

# Print the generated SignalFlow without calling the API.
sfx-olly query example.project.size --filter environment=env-test --dry-run

# Run SignalFlow copied from a chart file.
sfx-olly signalflow --file chart.flow --range 1h --resolution 1m

# Inspect active incidents or detector configurations.
sfx-olly incidents list
sfx-olly detectors list --limit 20

# Get command help or machine-readable results.
sfx-olly query --help
sfx-olly -o json metrics inspect example.project.size

--unit kib assumes the source values are bytes; it only formats table output. Add --latest to display the latest non-null returned point per series in the window. This can be an older sample, not proof of current availability.

docs.title: Understand Query Options
docs.text:
Option Question it answers --filter KEY=VALUE Which dimension-labelled series should be included? --range 1h How far back from now should the query look? --resolution 1m How large should each requested time bucket be? --rollup max How should one series' samples be combined within a bucket? --agg sum How should different series be combined at each timestamp? --by project.name Should that aggregation run separately for each project? --transform mean --over 1h Should each resulting series have a moving time calculation?

Start without aggregation and add it only when the result has the meaning you want. For example, summing duplicate reports of a shared project size would double-count it.

The Command Guide contains worked numeric examples, every option, a step-by-step project query, recipes, and dashboard comparison checks.

docs.title: Webhook Receiver
docs.text:
Set WEBHOOK_SHARED_SECRET in your local .env to a locally generated secret, and keep WEBHOOK_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE=true. Use that same secret in Splunk's webhook integration. Then start the receiver:

sfx-olly webhook serve

In another terminal, send a signed synthetic alert:

sfx-olly webhook send-test

The displayed Critical CPU alert is sample data, not an incident from your detector. serve listens for notifications; it does not create or trigger Splunk alerts.

Splunk needs a reachable HTTPS endpoint ending in /webhooks/splunk, not your laptop's localhost. Configure that integration as your detector's alert recipient. The webhook setup and end-to-end tests cover secrets, ngrok, local/tunnel/Splunk tests, payload storage, and 404/401 troubleshooting.

docs.title: Library Usage
docs.text:
from sfx_olly import SplunkOllyClient
from sfx_olly.metrics import MetricQuery
from sfx_olly.utils import time_range

start, stop = time_range("1h")
spec = MetricQuery("example.project.size", filters={"environment": ["env-test"]})
with SplunkOllyClient() as client:
    points = client.signalflow.query(spec, start, stop)

See the library reference for metadata APIs, custom settings, error handling, and webhook handlers.

docs.title: Scope and boundaries
docs.text:
The package currently supports metric discovery/queries, detectors/incidents, and receiving detector notifications. There is no watcher or metric-availability polling service. Use a Splunk-managed detector with webhook delivery for known-stream availability alerts; the receiver does not subscribe to a catalog of new metric names.

Metric-specific implementations live in sfx_olly/metrics/. Shared authentication, HTTP pooling, retries, pagination, and errors stay separate so another signal can reuse them without importing metric query builders. No empty traces/logs packages are scaffolded.

docs.title: Query flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Entry[CLI entry point or python -m sfx_olly] --> Main[cli/main.py: parse and dispatch]
    Main --> Discover[cli/metadata.py: search or inspect]
    Main --> Query[cli/data.py: query]
    Query --> Builder[metrics/query_builder.py: MetricQuery to SignalFlow]
    Builder --> Dry{dry-run?}
    Dry -->|yes| Program[Print program and exit]
    Dry -->|no| Client[api/client.py: shared client]
    Discover --> Client
    Client --> Metadata[metrics/metadata.py]
    Client --> SignalFlow[metrics/signalflow.py]
    Client --> Raw[metrics/timeseries.py]
    Metadata --> HTTP[api/http.py: authenticated HTTPS]
    SignalFlow --> HTTP
    Raw --> HTTP
    HTTP --> Splunk[Splunk Observability APIs]
    Splunk --> Responses[JSON metadata or SSE query results]
    Responses --> Output[cli/output.py: tables or JSON; inspect uses a tree]
    Config[config.py: env and .env] --> Client
    Config --> Main

metrics inspect issues one bounded MTS search and groups dimension values locally. query posts one program, consumes the finite historical SSE result, then exits. Explicit pagination in library iterators retrieves additional pages, not repeated checks waiting for new metrics. HTTP retries are bounded recovery from transient failures.

docs.title: Metric mental model
docs.text:
metric: example.project.size
  series A
    dimensions: {environment: env-test, project.name: project-a, ...}
    datapoints: [(timestamp, value), ...]
  series B
    dimensions: {environment: env-prod, project.name: project-b, ...}
    datapoints: [(timestamp, value), ...]

A metric name is not a single number. Each distinct dimension set identifies a metric time series (MTS). Dots in keys are literal: host.name is one flat key, not a nested object. Dimension inspection groups values across series, not a Cartesian product of valid filters. Use MTS search to examine combinations. Global dimension search can return keys/values belonging to other metrics, so it is not a substitute for per-metric inspection.

Metadata indicates indexed objects, not that samples exist in a selected time range. There is no exhaustive list of never-created metrics. Compare an explicit expected inventory with observed metadata, then query values separately when checking recent activity.

docs.title: Webhook flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Detector[Splunk detector triggers or clears] -->|HTTPS POST| App[webhook/app.py]
    App --> Checks[Size and content type; CIDR; HMAC signature]
    Checks --> Model[webhook/models.py: AlertPayload]
    Model --> Dedupe[webhook/security.py: replay guard]
    Dedupe --> Reply[HTTP accepted or duplicate]
    Dedupe --> Background[Background handlers for accepted alerts]
    Background --> Console[formatter.py and console handler]
    Background --> File[JSONL handler or custom sink]

This is an inbound notification path, independent of metric querying. HMAC uses WEBHOOK_SHARED_SECRET; outbound Splunk API requests use SFX_TOKEN. The receiver's background handlers and in-process replay guard are not a durable queue or global dedupe.

docs.title: Adding Another Signal
docs.text:
1. Create a signal-specific package such as sfx_olly/traces/ only when implementing it.
  2. Check that signal's actual Splunk API, token permissions, query format, and retention. Do not reuse metric data() or /v2/metric for raw traces or logs.
  3. Reuse HttpTransport and shared errors where compatible; add a specialized transport only if the signal's protocol requires one.
  4. Attach its API object to SplunkOllyClient and register an independent CLI module.
  5. Add focused mocked tests and document the new signal's own filters and result model.

The existing client attributes and sfx_olly.api exports remain supported. Direct imports from the former metric-specific API submodules must use the new sfx_olly.metrics paths.

docs.title: Command Guide
docs.text: Start here if metrics, dimensions, SignalFlow, or the command options are unfamiliar. Examples use fictional project-size metrics, but the commands work with other queryable numeric metrics. Names such as example.project.size, example.bytes.total, project-demo, and env-test are placeholders. Replace them with your own discovered metric/dimension values to return data. No organization-specific names or operational results are required. All numbers in the teaching tables are illustrative, not measurements from your system.

docs.title: Start with these commands
docs.text:
Complete the installation and configuration first. Run commands from the project directory if your settings are in its .env file. Never paste your API token or webhook secret into a support message.

# Find metric names using a fictional example prefix.
sfx-olly metrics search 'example.*'

# Discover which dimension keys and values exist for this metric.
sfx-olly metrics inspect example.project.size

# Read one project's individual series, without aggregation.
sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test \
  --filter project.name=project-demo \
  --range 1h --resolution 1m --unit kib

The last command assumes the metric's source values are bytes. It returns historical values, not a live subscription. If you only need the latest non-null value per series within that hour, append --latest. If the command returns no data, discover the dimensions first and then try a wider range; do not add aggregation to fix an empty filter.

If sfx-olly is not found, replace it with python -m sfx_olly, using the Python environment in which the project dependencies are installed.

docs.title: Metric, dimension, series, and datapoint
docs.text:
Term Plain meaning Example Metric The name of something being measured. example.project.size Dimension key A label that identifies which thing was measured. project.name, environment, host.name Dimension value The value of one of those labels. project-demo, env-test Metric time series (MTS) One metric plus a particular dimension set. Project A on host 1 in test Datapoint A value attached to a timestamp in a series. At 10:00 UTC, size was 102400 bytes Metadata Information describing metrics or series, not their numeric history. Metric type, description, dimension keys 
Metric: example.project.size
  Series 1: environment=test, project.name=A, host.name=host-1
    10:00 -> 100 KiB
    10:01 -> 120 KiB
  Series 2: environment=test, project.name=A, host.name=host-2
    10:00 -> 200 KiB
    10:01 -> 220 KiB
  Series 3: environment=test, project.name=B, host.name=host-1
    10:00 ->  50 KiB
    10:01 ->  60 KiB

One project can have several series because hosts or other dimensions differ. Filtering by project does not necessarily select just one series.

Dimensions are a flat map, not nested folders. deployment.environment.name is a literal key; it is not the same key as environment, env, or clusterName. Names and values should be copied exactly from discovery results, including case.

The inspection tree groups observed values for readability. It does not guarantee that every displayed project exists with every displayed host or environment.

docs.title: Read a command
docs.text:
sfx-olly query example.project.size --filter environment=env-test --range 1h

Read it as: "Fetch values of example.project.size, keep series labelled environment=env-test, and look back one hour from now."

Part What it does sfx-olly Starts this tool. query Selects the metric-values command. example.project.size Supplies the required metric name. --filter Introduces a dimension condition. --range Introduces the historical look-back period.

In multiline examples, a final backslash continues the same shell command on the next line. Do not put spaces after that backslash. You can also enter the whole command on one line, without the backslashes.

docs.title: Discover names and dimensions
docs.text:
# First page of indexed metric names, not datapoint values.
sfx-olly metrics search
sfx-olly metrics search 'example.*' --limit 100

# Metric metadata, including type when supplied by Splunk.
sfx-olly metrics get example.project.size

# A readable dimension tree for this metric.
sfx-olly metrics inspect example.project.size

# All observed values from the inspected series, in JSON.
sfx-olly -o json metrics inspect example.project.size --limit 2000

# Dimension combinations on individual series, not independent value lists.
sfx-olly mts search 'sf_metric:example.project.size AND environment:env-test'

# Global dimension search: may include dimensions from other metrics.
sfx-olly dimensions search 'key:host.name' --limit 50

inspect examines at most 1000 series by default, with a maximum of 10000. It labels partial inventories. The tree displays at most 10 values per key; JSON includes all values found in the inspected subset.

Search commands return 50 results by default. --limit 50 --offset 50 requests the next page after the first 50 results. Keep offset plus limit at or below 10000. inspect has --limit but no --offset option.

There are two different syntaxes:

Command Syntax Example metrics search Metadata search expression 'name:example.*' mts search / timeseries Series search expression 'sf_metric:example.project.size AND environment:env-test' query --filter Dimension key equals value --filter environment=env-test

Bare metric names in search commands get a default field automatically. Use quoted full search expressions for more complex conditions. A metric that was never ingested cannot be discovered by listing "unavailable" names; compare with an expected inventory. Indexed metadata can remain even when there are no recent samples.

docs.title: Filters: choose the right series
docs.text:
Filters select input series before calculations. They do not change numeric values.

# Both conditions must match: environment AND project.
sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test \
  --filter project.name=project-demo

# Either environment may match: test OR production.
sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test,env-prod

# Wildcard value: quote it to prevent shell wildcard expansion.
sfx-olly query example.project.size --filter 'project.name=METRICS_*'

# Keep test but exclude one project.
sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test \
  --exclude project.name=project-demo

Different included keys are combined with AND. Values for the same key are combined with OR, including when that key is repeated in multiple --filter options. --exclude removes matches; comma-separated values exclude any matching value. The convenience parser uses commas as separators, so a literal comma inside a dimension value needs custom SignalFlow rather than this option format. Quotes, backslashes, and control characters inside filter values are rejected by the builder. Shell quoting does not remove those builder restrictions.

docs.title: Range: how far back to look
docs.text:
--range answers: which historical period do I want?

The default is 15m. --range 1h means from one hour ago until now, not "return one average for the hour" and not "keep running for an hour".

Value Look back 30s 30 seconds 15m 15 minutes 1h 1 hour 2d 2 days 1w 1 week

Durations use positive whole numbers with s, m, h, d, or w. There is no month unit; m always means minutes. Use 90m, not 1.5h. The CLI currently has no absolute --start / --end options. Separate runs have slightly different end times because each ends at its own current time.

docs.title: Resolution: the size of a time bucket
docs.text:
--resolution answers: how finely should time be represented?

The default is 1m. Roughly speaking, --range 1h --resolution 1m asks for minute-sized buckets over an hour. It is not a request to wait a minute between HTTP calls. This tool does not poll for values.

Example Approximate buckets per output series --range 1h --resolution 1m 60 --range 1h --resolution 5m 12 --range 1d --resolution 1h 24

These are intuition, not guaranteed row counts. Splunk can adjust the actual resolution based on retention and availability; boundary alignment, sparse samples, and calculations also affect output. A one-minute request cannot create one-minute data from a source that reports hourly. The supported requested interval is 1 second through 1 day, inclusive.

Start with a resolution much smaller than your range and match the dashboard when comparing values. With --range 1h --resolution 16h, one requested bucket is larger than the entire requested period. Coarse, aligned buckets can be labelled outside the selected hour and are not directly comparable to a fine-resolution chart hover value. The CLI currently allows this combination; it does not automatically correct it.

docs.title: Rollup: samples inside one bucket
docs.text:
--rollup chooses how raw observations for each individual series are reduced to values at the requested resolution. If omitted, Splunk chooses its default based on the metric type; this CLI does not force average or latest.

Suppose a size gauge reports 100, 120, and 140 KiB inside one five-minute bucket:

Rollup Result for this teaching example Interpretation average 120 KiB Typical sampled size in the bucket. min 100 KiB Smallest sampled size. max 140 KiB Largest sampled size. latest 140 KiB Last sample in the bucket. sum 360 KiB Sum of the readings, usually not meaningful as current project size. count 3 Number of samples, not number of hosts or projects.

The table assumes all three samples are available and applicable to that rollup. Not every rollup is valid or meaningful for every source type. The CLI accepts these names, but Splunk ultimately decides whether a request is supported:

Rollup Use or caution average, min, max, latest Common gauge comparisons; choose the same one as the chart. sum, count Sum observations or count observations inside buckets; output meaning changes. delta Counter change/increment semantics; appropriate to supported counter data, not a generic way to subtract gauge endpoints. rate Counter activity per unit time, normally per second; verify source and API semantics. lag Specialized reporting-lag information, not the original metric magnitude; avoid for ordinary size comparisons. 
# Largest observed project size in each requested five-minute bucket.
sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test \
  --filter project.name=project-demo \
  --range 1h --resolution 5m --rollup max --unit kib

Do not choose sum just because a metric has "total" in its name. Inspect its type and the producer's definition first.

docs.title: Aggregation: combine different series
docs.text:
--agg answers: at each output timestamp, how should different matching series be combined? It does not add together all timestamps in the requested range.

Without --agg, each matching series is returned separately.

Suppose three independent inputs have values 100, 200, and 300 at the same timestamp:

--agg Result Meaning sum 600 Add the three inputs. mean 200 Arithmetic average of the inputs. min 100 Smallest input. max 300 Largest input. count 3 Number of contributing series values, not their sum. median 200 Middle input when sorted. stddev Spread, in the input's units Standard deviation; not a sum or typical value. variance Spread, in squared input units Variance; not a size in bytes or KiB.

This example assumes three present inputs. Missing values, extrapolation in custom programs, and backend function rules can change which inputs contribute. Do not use these counts as a guaranteed inventory of configured hosts.

# Largest matching project-size series at each output timestamp.
sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test \
  --agg max --range 1h --resolution 1m --unit kib

# Number of contributing series at each timestamp; leave the unit raw.
sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test \
  --agg count --range 1h --resolution 1m

Aggregation is a business decision, not just a display preference. Summing two hosts that report the same shared project size would double-count that size. Summing distinct independent contributions may be correct. Only the metric producer can establish whether the inputs are additive. Likewise, averaging percentages from unequal-capacity hosts is not necessarily a capacity-weighted utilization.

With exactly one contributing series, sum/mean/min/max have the same value at that timestamp. count would still produce a count, not the original value.

docs.title: Grouping: one answer per project or host
docs.text:
--by divides series into groups before applying --agg. It is not another filter. With no grouping, the aggregation combines all matching series into one result stream. With grouping, it produces a stream for each observed group.

Using the three series from the earlier teaching example, at 10:00:

Options Result No --agg A/host-1=100, A/host-2=200, B/host-1=50 --agg sum One combined result: 350 --agg sum --by project.name A=300, B=50 --agg sum --by host.name host-1=150, host-2=200 --agg sum --by project.name --by host.name Separate results for each observed project/host pair 
# One total per project, if the underlying series are genuinely additive.
sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test \
  --agg sum --by project.name --range 1h --resolution 1m --unit kib

Use --by once per key: --by project.name --by host.name. A comma-separated --by project.name,host.name is not this CLI's grouping syntax. --by requires --agg; the builder rejects grouping on its own. Discover the key first and check series where the grouping dimension is missing. Grouping can remove the identity of individual input series, so inspect unaggregated results when you need to understand exactly which hosts contributed.

docs.title: Transform: calculate over time
docs.text:
--transform plus --over answers: for each output series, how should values over a moving historical window be combined?

The window is evaluated at each output timestamp. It is not automatically one final answer for the entire --range and is not a calendar-day report.

# For each input series, show a moving one-hour average project size.
sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test \
  --range 6h --resolution 5m --transform mean --over 1h --unit kib

# First choose the largest input at each timestamp, then its moving one-hour max.
sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test \
  --agg max --range 6h --resolution 5m \
  --transform max --over 1h --unit kib

For an illustrative sequence 100, 120, 140, a moving sum over a window containing all three values would be 360, while its moving mean would be 120. Summing size-gauge readings normally does not mean "current size" or "bytes transferred".

Both options must be supplied together. The allowed function names are the same as the aggregation choices, but actual support and statistical/window behavior depend on SignalFlow. The window format here is a positive integer of at most five digits followed by lowercase s, m, h, d, or w. Use custom SignalFlow for calculations that need different ordering, calendar windows, weighting, or unsupported functions. Splunk may need history before the requested start to initialize a moving calculation; missing history can affect early outputs.

docs.title: The order of operations
docs.text:
Choose metric and matching dimension sets
  -> roll up each input series to the requested resolution
  -> aggregate across series, optionally grouped by dimension
  -> transform each resulting series over a moving time window
  -> publish results
  -> optionally display only the latest non-null point per output series
  -> format numbers for display

--range determines the historical output period. --resolution controls the requested granularity; it is not a fourth aggregation function.

These operations are not interchangeable. For example, "maximum host value over time" and "sum of each host's maximum" can differ because the hosts may peak at different timestamps. The builder's order is fixed. Inspect it without API access:

sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test \
  --rollup max --agg sum --by project.name \
  --transform mean --over 1h --dry-run

The generated program is:

data('example.project.size', filter=filter('environment', 'env-test'), rollup='max').sum(by=['project.name']).mean(over='1h').publish(label='A')

This is SignalFlow syntax, not a Python script to run with the Python interpreter. It means: within each bucket take each input's maximum; sum those values per project; then compute a moving one-hour mean for each resulting project stream.

docs.title: Gauges, counters, and choosing a calculation
docs.text:
Measurement Often represented as Starting approach Current project size, temperature, utilization Gauge: value can rise or fall. Start without aggregation; match chart average/max/latest rollup. Events recorded per reporting interval Counter: interval increments. Check the metric definition and supported rollup; don't differentiate increments again. Lifetime bytes or requests Cumulative counter: generally rises, but can reset. Use a backend-supported change/rate calculation appropriate to the source. Histogram buckets or summaries Several numeric metrics or specialized distributions. Query numeric series carefully; do not assume bucket totals are percentiles.

Metric names alone are insufficient. For these examples, assume example.project.size is a GAUGE reporting bytes. Check your real metric's type and confirm its unit from the collector/application before applying a byte display unit. Metadata may not specify a unit.

For cumulative readings 1000, 1100, 1250, adding them gives 3350, not the increase. The simple endpoint increase is 250 if no reset occurred. Real counter queries also need to handle resets, sample timing, and the producer's metric conventions.

Your question Consider What did this one series report? No --agg or --transform initially. What is the largest independent input at each timestamp? --agg max What is the total of additive inputs per project? --agg sum --by project.name What is the typical value across equally weighted input series? --agg mean What is the average of each series over the previous hour? --transform mean --over 1h What was the largest raw reading within each time bucket? --rollup max What was the last available returned value per series? --latest, a display selection rather than a calculation.

docs.title: Units, timestamps, and latest values
docs.text:
--unit affects table display only. It does not change the query, guess the metric's source unit, change timestamps, or make results equivalent to a dashboard calculation.

Option Behavior, assuming the source is bytes --unit raw Print the numeric API value without byte conversion; default. --unit kib Divide by 1024 and display KiB. --unit mib Divide by 1048576 and display MiB. --unit gib Divide by 1073741824 and display GiB. --unit bytes Choose B, KiB, MiB, or GiB automatically based on magnitude.

For example, 114688 bytes = 112 KiB. Decimal kB uses a factor of 1000, not 1024; that difference is small and cannot explain a difference like 310 versus 112. If the source already reports KiB, dividing it by 1024 again would be incorrect. Use raw units for counts, percentages, and variance unless you explicitly know the intended conversion. JSON remains raw even when a display unit is requested.

Output timestamps are UTC. Bucket timestamps represent a computation interval, not necessarily the exact arrival time of a raw sample. Check the dashboard timezone.

--latest selects the last non-null returned point for each output series. It does not select the maximum, fill gaps, or keep only one series overall. With a two-day range it can show a sample from yesterday. It does not prove the metric is reporting now. An actual zero value is retained and is not considered missing.

docs.title: Your project-size query, step by step
docs.text: Start without calculations, then add only the ones that answer your question.

docs.title: Step 1: Check the project and environment
docs.text:
sfx-olly mts search 'sf_metric:example.project.size AND environment:env-test AND project.name:project-demo'

Look at how many series match and their full dimension sets. One project can have multiple hosts. Do not assume one series just because the filter names one project.

docs.title: Step 2: Inspect historical values
docs.text:
sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test \
  --filter project.name=project-demo \
  --range 1h --resolution 1m --unit kib

This does not specify a rollup, so Splunk chooses the metric's default. Compare actual timestamps and values, not just the last number on the screen.

docs.title: Step 3: Reduce the display, not the calculation
docs.text:
sfx-olly query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test \
  --filter project.name=project-demo \
  --range 1h --resolution 1m --unit kib --latest

docs.title: Step 4: Add a calculation only if needed
docs.text: If distinct additive inputs exist and the question is "total per project at each timestamp", add --agg sum --by project.name. If inputs are duplicate reports of the same shared size, sum is not correct. If you need no cross-series combination, leave both options off. Changing aggregation to force a match with the UI hides the cause.

docs.title: Step 5: Understand your original command
docs.text:
--filter environment=env-test       Select the test environment.
--filter project.name=project-demo
                                         Also select this exact project.
--range 1h                               Ask for the preceding hour.
--unit kib                               Display bytes divided by 1024.
--agg sum --by project.name                  Sum matching inputs per project at each timestamp.
--resolution 16h                         Ask for buckets much larger than that hour.

For illustration, a coarse bucket might show 300 KiB while a finer bucket shows 120 KiB because they summarize different samples. Those teaching numbers are not results from your account. With one contributing series, sum and no aggregation match at the same timestamp; different bucket sizes can still produce different values. Compare the dashboard's exact timestamp, rollup, and resolution first.

docs.title: What are all the matching projects reporting individually?
docs.text:
sfx-olly query example.project.size --filter environment=env-test \
  --range 2d --resolution 5m --unit kib --latest

This can still return multiple series for the same project. It does not merge hosts.

docs.title: What is the peak reported value per project at each timestamp?
docs.text:
sfx-olly query example.project.size --filter environment=env-test \
  --agg max --by project.name --range 1d --resolution 5m --unit kib

This takes the maximum across input series per project at each bucket. It is not one maximum over the entire day. --resolution 5m may itself hide within-bucket peaks if the source/default rollup averages; add --rollup max only if that is the supported calculation you want.

docs.title: What is the byte rate per topic for a supported counter?
docs.text:
sfx-olly query example.bytes.total \
  --filter environment=env-prod \
  --rollup rate --agg sum --by topic --range 1h --resolution 1m

Use this only after confirming the source is a counter for which Splunk's rate rollup has the intended semantics. A name ending in total is not sufficient proof. If the input counts bytes and the rate is per second, the result means bytes per second, not total bytes over the hour. It intentionally uses raw display units. Verify that producers are distinct contributions before summing them; duplicate reporters can double-count rates too. Counter resets and reporting intervals matter.

docs.title: What is the moving peak per project over the previous hour?
docs.text:
sfx-olly query example.project.size --filter environment=env-test \
  --rollup max --agg max --by project.name \
  --transform max --over 1h --range 6h --resolution 5m --unit kib

This intentionally uses maximum at all three calculation stages. Each output point summarizes its preceding hour; there are still several output timestamps.

docs.title: How do I export results as JSON?
docs.text:
sfx-olly -o json query example.project.size \
  --filter environment=env-test --range 1h --latest

-o json is a global option and belongs before query. The JSON contains numeric values, timestamps in milliseconds, series IDs, and properties. Do not combine --show-program with JSON when you need stdout to contain only JSON: that option also prints the program to stdout. Use a separate --dry-run command instead.

docs.title: How do I inspect the request without querying Splunk?
docs.text:
sfx-olly query example.project.size --filter environment=env-test \
  --agg max --by project.name --dry-run

--dry-run prints SignalFlow and makes no API call. It validates the builder inputs, but does not prove the metric exists or that Splunk supports the requested calculation. Range/resolution are request parameters, not part of the printed program; the dry-run path does not validate those parameters. For endpoint and request timing diagnostics:

sfx-olly -v query example.project.size --filter environment=env-test \
  --range 1h --resolution 1m --latest

Verbose mode makes a real request and logs diagnostics to stderr. The token is redacted, but query text and business dimension values can still be sensitive.

docs.title: Every query option
docs.text:
Option Default What to remember Metric name Required Numeric metric to fetch; wildcard patterns are allowed. --filter KEY=V[,V] None Keep matching dimensions; repeat for more keys. --exclude KEY=V[,V] None Remove matching dimensions. --range DURATION 15m Historical output period ending now. --resolution DURATION 1m Requested time-bucket interval, 1s through 1d. --rollup NAME Backend default Per-series treatment within a bucket. --agg NAME No aggregation Cross-series calculation at each timestamp. --by DIMENSION No grouping Requires --agg; repeat once per grouping key. --transform NAME No transform Moving time calculation; requires --over. --over DURATION None Moving window; requires --transform. --latest Off Display latest non-null point per output series in the window. --unit raw/bytes/kib/mib/gib raw Display formatting only; JSON stays raw. --label NAME A SignalFlow output label; does not filter input dimensions. --show-program Off Print generated SignalFlow, then execute it. --dry-run Off Print generated SignalFlow and exit without an API call. -h, --help Off Show this command's option summary.

Aggregation and transform choices: mean, sum, min, max, count, median, stddev, variance. Rollup choices: average, sum, min, max, count, delta, rate, latest, lag. These are accepted builder names, not a guarantee of every function/source/window combination at the API.

The naming difference is intentional: the rollup choice is average, while the cross-series aggregation and moving-transform choice is mean. For example, --rollup average --agg mean first averages samples per input bucket and then averages those resulting values across input series.

Labels allow letters, digits, underscores, and hyphens, up to 64 characters. For dimension names, use those found by inspection; the convenience builder permits letters, digits, underscores, dots, colons, slashes, and hyphens (up to 128 characters). Other valid source names/values may require custom SignalFlow if this builder rejects them.

Global options go before the command:

Option Meaning -o table Default readable tables, or a tree for metric inspection. -o json Machine-readable results; query values stay raw. -v, --verbose Log requests and timings to stderr; not live polling. --version Show the installed toolkit version. --help Show the command list.

metrics get, detectors get, and incidents get always print JSON. Global output selection does not turn the webhook receiver into a raw-JSON console stream; use its JSONL output file for saved payloads.

docs.title: Discovery option reference
docs.text:
Command Inputs and options Result metrics search Optional search text (default *); --limit (50), --offset (0). Indexed metric metadata, not samples. metrics get Required metric name. Full metric metadata as JSON. metrics inspect Required metric name; --limit (1000). Dimension tree or JSON; reports partial inventories. dimensions search Required search text; --limit (50), --offset (0). Global dimension metadata, not scoped to one metric. mts search Required search text; --limit (50), --offset (0). Individual matching series and their dimension combinations. 
# Request the next 50 results, skipping the first page.
sfx-olly metrics search 'example.*' --limit 50 --offset 50

docs.title: Run SignalFlow copied from the UI
docs.text:
sfx-olly signalflow "data('cpu.utilization').mean(by=['host']).publish()" \
  --range 1h --resolution 1m
sfx-olly signalflow --file chart.flow --range 1h --resolution 1m --unit kib

The file example assumes your copied program exists at that path. There is no reverse-conversion requirement: the tool sends the program directly to SignalFlow. Use either positional program text or --file, not both. File size is bounded at 50000 bytes; the program text also has a length limit.

The program must publish the desired output. Resolve UI-specific arguments and dashboard variables first; this CLI has no --program-args option. Keep only the intended enabled outputs. Custom SignalFlow may perform its own scaling, so check that you are not converting bytes to KiB twice. Supported display options are --latest and --unit; builder options such as --agg belong inside the custom program, not after signalflow on the command line.

docs.title: Raw time-series window
docs.text:
sfx-olly timeseries 'sf_metric:example.project.size AND environment:env-test' \
  --range 1h --resolution 5m --last 3

timeseries uses a different raw-data API rather than generating SignalFlow. --last 3 shows the last three returned points per series in table output; it does not reduce the fetched window. JSON still contains the complete response data. Its default --last is 5. This command has no --unit, --agg, or --latest option. Use query for dimension-labelled analytics and unit formatting.

docs.title: Detectors and incidents
docs.text:
Both plural and singular command names work: incidents / incident and detectors / detector. They are aliases with identical list/get behavior.

sfx-olly detectors list --name CPU --limit 20
sfx-olly detectors list --tag production --limit 20
sfx-olly detectors get YOUR_DETECTOR_ID
sfx-olly incidents list
sfx-olly incidents list --include-resolved --limit 100
sfx-olly incidents get YOUR_INCIDENT_ID
sfx-olly incident list
sfx-olly detector list --limit 20

A detector is an alerting rule configuration. An incident is an occurrence of that rule firing. These commands retrieve metadata; they do not create a detector or acknowledge an incident. Replace YOUR_DETECTOR_ID / YOUR_INCIDENT_ID with an ID returned by the respective list command; an ID is not the display name.

Option or input Applies to Meaning --name TEXT detectors list Name substring filter. --tag TAG detectors list Detector tag filter. --include-resolved incidents list Also request resolved incidents; default listing is active-only. --limit N Both list commands Max results for this request; default 50. --offset N Both list commands Number of results to skip; default 0. Required ID Both get commands Retrieve one detector/incident, printed as JSON.

docs.title: Webhook receiver and tests
docs.text:
sfx-olly webhook serve

Run the following in another terminal while the receiver stays running:

sfx-olly webhook send-test
sfx-olly webhook send-test --state ok

Unlike historical queries, webhook serve is a long-running HTTP listener. It receives notifications, rather than polling Splunk. send-test creates a synthetic CPU critical alert, not a detector or a real incident in your Splunk organization. The two commands do not automatically subscribe you to every detector.

Configure the shared secret, public HTTPS URL, and detector recipient using the webhook setup and local/tunnel/Splunk test sequence. Use webhook render to display saved JSON/JSONL alerts. Configure WEBHOOK_OUTPUT_FILE to preserve payloads; console output is a formatted summary.

Option or input Applies to Meaning --url URL webhook send-test Override the derived local URL, for example to test through ngrok. Include the webhook path. --file PATH webhook send-test Send your existing JSON payload file instead of generating the sample. --state STATE webhook send-test Sample state: anomalous (default), ok, manually resolved, or stopped. Quote values containing spaces. --insecure webhook send-test Skip TLS certificate verification for isolated self-signed local tests only. Do not use for ngrok or production. Required file path webhook render Read an existing .json or .jsonl alert file and display it. No API query. WEBHOOK_* settings webhook serve Configure secret, host, port, output, and security through env/.env, not --port or --secret CLI options.

--state controls the generated sample; it does not rewrite a supplied --file payload. Both file-based operations limit input file size to 50 MiB.

sfx-olly webhook send-test --state 'manually resolved'
sfx-olly webhook send-test --file my-payload.json
sfx-olly webhook render ./data/alerts.jsonl

The last two examples require those files to exist; the JSONL file is only created when file output is configured and notifications are received.

docs.title: Offline help
docs.text:
sfx-olly help
sfx-olly help query
sfx-olly help signalflow
sfx-olly query --help
sfx-olly metrics inspect --help

Help and dry-run work without API credentials. Help text lists options; this guide explains which question each option answers and how the operations interact.

docs.title: Match a dashboard and troubleshoot
docs.text:
Use this comparison sequence rather than changing several options at once:

  1. Confirm the same organization/realm and API permissions.
  2. Copy the metric and filter keys exactly; inspect series and dimension combinations.
  3. Match the chart's time range, UTC timestamps, and actual resolution. A chart hover is one timestamp, not the latest sample from a later CLI execution.
  4. Compare the chart's rollup. An average bucket can differ from its maximum or last sample.
  5. Compare cross-series aggregation and grouping. Check for duplicate reporters.
  6. Compare time transforms, formulas, weighting, extrapolation, and unit conversion.
  7. Run the chart's actual SignalFlow if the simple builder cannot express its logic.
  8. Compare raw values before formatting; then apply the same display unit.

No data does not mean zero, and it does not prove the metric never existed. Filters, range, sparse reporting, token visibility, and retained metadata are separate checks. Avoid automatic fill/extrapolation just to make a result resemble the UI.

Symptom First check Empty result Remove one filter at a time; inspect dimensions; widen range if appropriate. Number larger than UI Bucket size/rollup, summed duplicate series, transformations, units. Multiple rows for one project Other dimensions identify distinct series or multiple timestamps remain. One old row with --latest It is the last available non-null point in the range, not necessarily current. --by error Supply --agg and repeat --by separately for each key. Transform/window error Supply both --transform and --over. Unrecognized global option position Put -o json / -v before query or another top-level command. HTTP 401/403 Check token API permissions and correct organization; do not share tokens. Webhook 404/401 Check URL path / shared-secret signature respectively; see webhook tests.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake Better approach Adding flags without deciding what the result should mean. Write the question first, then add one operation at a time. Using --range 1h --resolution 16h to compare a chart hover. Match chart resolution and keep buckets sensibly smaller than the range. Thinking --agg sum gives the total over the range. It sums series at each timestamp; time calculations are a different stage. Using --rollup sum to find current project size. A size is usually a gauge; inspect readings and match the chart's rollup. Treating a moving sum of gauge readings as transferred bytes. Use the appropriate transfer/counter metric and supported counter semantics. Thinking --latest means raw source sample or maximum. It selects the latest non-null returned output point after all calculations. Treating environment as an alias of deployment.environment.name. Use the literal keys present on the desired series. Applying byte units to counts or already-converted KiB. Check source and result units first. Running --dry-run and expecting datapoints. Dry-run only prints generated SignalFlow. Expecting local webhook send-test to validate Splunk delivery. Test local, public tunnel, and Splunk integration separately.

For module ownership and implementation flows, see Architecture. For environment variables, deployment/security considerations, and cURL examples, see the User Reference. Return to the README for the quick start.

docs.title: User Reference
docs.text:
A modular Python package to:

  • Query Splunk Observability Cloud (SignalFx) REST APIs: metrics, dimensions, MTS, raw time series, SignalFlow, detectors and incidents.
  • Receive detector alert webhooks, verify their signature, and display them formatted in the terminal (and optionally store them as JSON Lines).
  • Use everything from a CLI (sfx-olly) or as a library in your own code.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
1. Project structure
  2. Installation
  3. Configuration
  4. CLI usage
  5. Webhook receiver
  6. Library usage
  7. Extending
  8. Security
  9. Scaling
  10. Troubleshooting
  11. License

New to these options? Start with the Command Guide. It explains metrics and dimensions, range versus resolution, rollup versus aggregation versus time transforms, every query option, and step-by-step project-size examples.

All metric, project, host, topic, and environment values in the examples are fictional. For example, example.project.size, example.bytes.total, project-demo, and env-test are placeholders, not built-in metrics. Replace them with names discovered in your own organization. Never substitute real credentials into committed examples.

docs.text:
sfx_olly/
├── __init__.py          # exports SplunkOllyClient
├── __main__.py          # python -m sfx_olly
├── config.py            # typed settings from env/.env (ApiSettings, WebhookSettings, LoggingSettings)
├── exceptions.py        # ApiError, AuthenticationError, NotFoundError, RateLimitError, SignalFlowError
├── logging_config.py    # text/JSON logging with secret redaction
├── utils.py             # durations, time ranges, validation helpers
├── help.py              # built-in help topics (sfx-olly help <topic>)
├── api/
│   ├── http.py          # shared HTTP transport: auth, TLS, retries, error mapping
│   ├── base.py          # BaseAPI + pagination
│   ├── alerts.py        # detectors, incidents
│   └── client.py        # SplunkOllyClient facade
├── metrics/
│   ├── __init__.py      # public metric API exports
│   ├── metadata.py      # metric/MTS search and dimension inspection
│   ├── timeseries.py    # /v1/timeserieswindow
│   ├── query_builder.py # MetricQuery -> safe SignalFlow program
│   └── signalflow.py    # one-shot SignalFlow execution (SSE)
├── webhook/
│   ├── models.py        # AlertPayload (pydantic)
│   ├── security.py      # HMAC signature, IP allowlist, replay guard
│   ├── formatter.py     # rich terminal rendering
│   ├── handlers.py      # pluggable sinks: console, JSONL file
│   ├── app.py           # FastAPI app factory
│   ├── server.py        # uvicorn runner
│   └── testing.py       # signed sample alert sender
└── cli/
    ├── main.py          # argument parser + error handling
    ├── output.py        # table / JSON output
    ├── metadata.py      # metrics, dimensions, mts commands
    ├── data.py          # query, timeseries, signalflow commands
    ├── alerts.py        # detectors, incidents commands
    ├── webhook.py       # webhook serve / send-test / render
    └── help_cmd.py      # help command

Each layer only depends on the one below it: CLI → API/Webhook → config/utils. You can reuse the API or webhook modules without the CLI.

See Architecture for every module's responsibility, call flows, and the plan for adding traces or other signals without mixing their APIs with metrics. Metric-specific imports now live in sfx_olly.metrics; existing from sfx_olly.api import MetricQuery and client.metadata / client.signalflow / client.timeseries still work. Direct imports such as sfx_olly.api.query_builder must change to sfx_olly.metrics.query_builder.

There is no watcher, local polling loop, state baseline, or WATCH_* configuration. Each discovery/query command runs once and exits. SSE delivers one query's results; it is not repeated polling for a metric to appear.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Requires Python 3.10+.

cd signalfx-playground
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .                 # installs the `sfx-olly` command
# or: pip install -r requirements.txt   (then use `python -m sfx_olly`)

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
All configuration is external. Values are read from environment variables, or from a .env file in the working directory. Real environment variables take precedence over .env.

cp .env.example .env
# edit .env: set SFX_TOKEN, SFX_REALM (and WEBHOOK_SHARED_SECRET for webhooks)

docs.title: CLI usage
docs.text:
For detailed explanations and worked numeric examples, read the beginner-friendly Command Guide. In particular:

  • Range: which historical period to query.
  • Resolution: how finely to divide time.
  • Rollup: combine one series' samples inside a bucket.
  • Aggregation: combine different series at each timestamp.
  • Grouping: calculate separately per project or host.
  • Transform: calculate over a moving time window.
  • Your project-size query: build and understand the command one step at a time.
sfx-olly --help                # all commands
sfx-olly <command> -h          # options for one command
sfx-olly help                  # list help topics
sfx-olly help webhook          # detailed guide for one topic

Global options:

Option Description -o table (default) Human-readable tables -o json Raw API JSON (pipe to jq) -v, --verbose Print each API endpoint (with query params), request body (e.g. SignalFlow) and response status/timing to stderr. The token is never printed. Put it before the command: sfx-olly -v query ... --version Show version

docs.title: Help module
docs.text:
The built-in help works offline and needs no token:

Topic Covers quickstart Install, configure, first query config Environment variables metrics Metric / dimension / MTS search query Fetch values of any metric (generic, no SignalFlow needed) timeseries Raw datapoints signalflow SignalFlow programs alerts Detectors and incidents webhook Webhook receiver setup security Security controls library Using the package from Python 
sfx-olly help signalflow

docs.title: Metrics, dimensions and MTS metadata
docs.text:
These commands return metadata (names, types, dimensions), not values. Search endpoints use field:value syntax. A bare term gets a default field added: metrics uses name:, dimensions uses key:, and mts/timeseries use sf_metric:.

sfx-olly metrics search example.bytes.total          # = name:example.bytes.total
sfx-olly metrics search "example.*" --limit 20
sfx-olly mts search "sf_metric:example.bytes.total AND environment:env-prod"

docs.title: Discover a metric and its dimensions
docs.text:
sfx-olly metrics search                         # indexed metric names (first 50)
sfx-olly metrics search 'example.*' --limit 100
sfx-olly metrics get example.project.size            # metric metadata, including type
sfx-olly metrics inspect example.project.size        # dimension keys -> observed values
sfx-olly -o json metrics inspect example.project.size
sfx-olly mts search 'sf_metric:example.project.size AND environment:env-test'

inspect reads at most 1,000 series by default, once. Increase --limit up to 10,000. It labels partial inventories; a value missing from a partial inventory is not proof of absence. The tree shows 10 values per key; JSON includes all values from the inspected series. Use --offset / --limit on searches to view subsequent pages (offset + limit <= 10,000).

Think metric name -> series -> dimension key/value set -> timestamped values. Dimensions are actually a flat map: environment and deployment.environment.name are distinct literal keys, not aliases or nested objects. The tree groups observed values for readability; it does not imply that every combination of values exists. Use mts search to see the dimensions that occur together on each series.

docs.title: Missing metrics and alternatives to polling
docs.text:
An API cannot list names that have never been sent: there is no inventory of all possible future metrics. Compare an expected-name list from your application/collector configuration against metrics search results to identify missing expected names. Search/get are one-shot checks:

sfx-olly metrics search 'name:expected.metric.name'
sfx-olly mts search 'sf_metric:expected.metric.name'
sfx-olly query expected.metric.name --range 2d --latest

These answer different questions: indexed name, indexed series, and values within a time window. A retained metadata entry does not mean a metric is reporting now. No datapoints can also mean a wrong filter, time range, realm/org, token visibility, or rollup. It does not establish that the metric never existed. There is no metrics search --unavailable catalog.

For notification without a local watcher, configure a Splunk-managed detector on a known metric/heartbeat and send its alerts to this package's webhook receiver. Use a no-data condition for a stream that stops reporting, or an appropriate presence/value condition for a known stream that starts reporting. A zero value may be valid, so do not equate zero with absence. For arbitrary new metric names, a detector/webhook is not a general metric-catalog change feed; the producer/collector must emit an explicit registration/event if you need that behavior without catalog polling. The receiver alone cannot detect new metric names.

docs.title: Generic metric query (values for any metric)
docs.text:
query turns options into a SignalFlow program, runs it, and prints the results. This is the generic way to get the values of any metric.

sfx-olly query example.bytes.total
sfx-olly query example.bytes.total --filter environment=env-prod --filter 'topic=*' --agg mean
sfx-olly query example.bytes.total --rollup delta --agg sum --by topic \
    --transform sum --over 1d --range 1d --resolution 1h --latest
sfx-olly query cpu.utilization --filter host=web-01,web-02 --exclude env=dev --agg max --by host --show-program
sfx-olly query cpu.utilization --agg mean --dry-run        # print SignalFlow only
Option Meaning --filter KEY=V[,V] Keep series whose dimension matches. Repeat the option for AND. Commas mean OR. * is a wildcard. --exclude KEY=V[,V] Drop series whose dimension matches. --rollup How raw points roll up: average, sum, min, max, count, delta, rate, latest, lag --agg / --by DIM Aggregate across series (mean, sum, min, max, count, median, stddev, variance), optionally grouped by a dimension. --transform / --over Aggregate over a time window, e.g. --transform sum --over 1d. --range / --resolution Look-back window and data granularity. --latest Show only the latest value per series. --unit How values are displayed: raw (default), bytes (auto B/KiB/MiB/GiB), kib, mib, gib. Tables only; -o json stays raw. --show-program / --dry-run Print the generated SignalFlow (--dry-run doesn't call the API).

The same thing from Python:

from sfx_olly import SplunkOllyClient
from sfx_olly.api import MetricQuery
from sfx_olly.utils import time_range

spec = MetricQuery(
    metric="example.bytes.total",
    filters={"environment": ["env-prod"]},
    rollup="delta", aggregation="sum", group_by=["topic"],
    transform="sum", window="1d",
)
start, end = time_range("1d")
with SplunkOllyClient() as client:
    for p in client.signalflow.query(spec, start, end, resolution_ms=3_600_000):
        print(p.timestamp_ms, p.properties.get("topic"), p.value)

The builder only accepts known functions and validated metric, dimension and window names. Filter values containing quotes, backslashes or control characters are rejected, so user input can't inject SignalFlow code.

docs.title: Metric types and other signals
docs.text:
Nothing is hardcoded to example telemetry, project-size, CPU, or a specific environment. The same builder works with queryable numeric metric series and their actual dimension keys, subject to the input validation above and API permissions. It does not choose the correct metric semantics for you:

Metric representation Query guidance Gauge (size, temperature, utilization) Read values; choose average/min/max/latest rollup to match the chart. Counter / cumulative counter Choose delta or rate when appropriate to the source's counter semantics; match the dashboard. A sum of cumulative readings is usually not a total increase. Histogram / summary exported as numeric bucket, count, sum series Query the exported numeric series; bucket counts are not automatically percentiles. Native distribution or specialized analytics Not guaranteed by this simple numeric builder. Use supported custom SignalFlow or add a distribution-specific API after checking the metric format. APM-derived metrics Work if exposed as ordinary metrics in the metric catalog; use their actual dimension keys. Raw traces, logs, profiles, events Not metric datapoints. These need their own signal-specific API modules and are not implemented here.

The --unit flag only formats numbers; it does not infer whether a metric is bytes, a count, or a percentage. Do not use --unit bytes unless the source value is measured in bytes.

docs.title: More metadata examples

docs.title: cURL POST: execute the same query
docs.text:
This is the SignalFlow execute API used by sfx-olly query, not a metric-ingestion API or the local alert receiver. Export SFX_TOKEN and SFX_REALM in your shell first; cURL does not load .env automatically. Use an API-scoped token for the same org as the dashboard. The example assumes a fictional metric with an environment dimension:

export SFX_REALM=us1
STOP_MS="$(($(date +%s) * 1000))"
START_MS="$((STOP_MS - 2 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000))"
curl --fail-with-body --no-buffer --request POST \
    "${SFX_STREAM_BASE_URL:-https://stream.${SFX_REALM}.signalfx.com}/v2/signalflow/execute?start=${START_MS}&stop=${STOP_MS}&resolution=60000&immediate=true" \
    --header "X-SF-Token: ${SFX_TOKEN:?Export SFX_TOKEN first}" \
    --header 'Content-Type: text/plain' \
    --header 'Accept: text/event-stream' \
    --data-binary "data('example.project.size', filter=filter('environment', 'env-test')).publish(label='A')"

The response is SSE (event: / data: blocks), not one JSON document. start and stop are Unix milliseconds. immediate=true returns available historical data without waiting for future samples. Do not use -k or -L; optionally supply --cacert "$SFX_CA_BUNDLE" for a corporate CA. See the SignalFlow API reference. For the separate inbound webhook POST, see signed cURL testing.

docs.title: Webhook receiver
docs.text: Splunk Observability can POST a JSON notification to your endpoint whenever a detector triggers or clears. The receiver checks each request, replies 200 straight away, and passes the alert to one or more handlers. By default the console handler shows it as a formatted panel.

docs.title: 1. Configure
docs.text:
python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"   # generate secret

In .env in the project directory, replace the placeholder with the generated value:

WEBHOOK_SHARED_SECRET=<generated value>
WEBHOOK_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE=true
WEBHOOK_OUTPUT_FILE=./data/alerts.jsonl     # optional: also store alerts

Run sfx-olly webhook serve from that directory so it can find .env. Configure the same secret in Splunk's webhook integration. Do not share the secret or commit .env.

docs.title: Missing shared-secret error
docs.text:
If startup reports:

WEBHOOK_SHARED_SECRET is required when WEBHOOK_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE=true

the receiver has no non-empty secret configured. Generate and set it as shown above, then start the receiver again. Keep signature verification enabled, especially when exposing the receiver through a public URL.

Environment variables override .env. If the error persists after updating .env, an empty exported variable may be overriding it. Remove that shell override and restart:

unset WEBHOOK_SHARED_SECRET
sfx-olly webhook serve
Variable Default Description WEBHOOK_HOST 127.0.0.1 Bind address. Use 0.0.0.0 inside containers. WEBHOOK_PORT 8080 Listen port. WEBHOOK_PATH /webhooks/splunk Endpoint path. WEBHOOK_WORKERS 1 Uvicorn worker processes. WEBHOOK_SHARED_SECRET – Must match the "Shared secret" in the Splunk integration. WEBHOOK_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE true Refuse to start without a secret. Set false only for local experiments. WEBHOOK_MAX_BODY_BYTES 262144 Reject larger bodies with 413. WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_CIDRS – Comma-separated source allowlist, e.g. 10.0.0.0/8,203.0.113.0/24. WEBHOOK_TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS false Use X-Forwarded-For (only behind a trusted proxy). WEBHOOK_FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS 127.0.0.1 Proxy IPs whose forwarded headers are trusted. WEBHOOK_DEDUPE_TTL_SECONDS 300 Ignore repeated deliveries of the same event (0 disables). WEBHOOK_CONSOLE_OUTPUT true Print formatted alerts to stdout. WEBHOOK_OUTPUT_FILE – Append alerts as JSON Lines (file mode 0600). WEBHOOK_SSL_CERTFILE / WEBHOOK_SSL_KEYFILE – Serve HTTPS directly instead of via a proxy.

docs.title: 2. Run and test locally
docs.text:
# terminal 1
sfx-olly webhook serve

# terminal 2 — send a signed sample alert
sfx-olly webhook send-test
sfx-olly webhook send-test --state ok
sfx-olly webhook send-test --file my-payload.json

webhook serve starts a listener that verifies, displays, and optionally saves incoming notifications. It does not create detectors or trigger alerts in Splunk. webhook send-test sends a synthetic Critical: CPU above 90% on web-01 alert by default. That sample is not a real Splunk incident and need not match any detector you configured. Its incident ID starts with TEST.

The default test URL is localhost, so a successful local test does not verify ngrok or Splunk delivery. Continue with the end-to-end webhook test.

docs.title: Signed cURL testing
docs.text:
For the local receiver API, start sfx-olly webhook serve, then export WEBHOOK_SHARED_SECRET in the calling shell with the same value as the receiver. Sign the exact body sent; this does not use SFX_TOKEN:

BODY='{"incidentId":"curl-test","status":"anomalous","severity":"Critical","detector":"cURL test","messageTitle":"Test alert"}'
SIGNATURE="$(printf '%s' "$BODY" | python -c 'import base64, hashlib, hmac, os, sys; print(base64.b64encode(hmac.new(os.environ["WEBHOOK_SHARED_SECRET"].encode(), sys.stdin.buffer.read(), hashlib.sha256).digest()).decode())')"
curl --fail-with-body --request POST \
    'http://127.0.0.1:8080/webhooks/splunk' \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "X-SFX-Signature: $SIGNATURE" \
    --data-binary "$BODY"

Use your configured port/path if different. Local HTTP is for localhost testing only; the endpoint registered with Splunk must be public HTTPS. sfx-olly webhook send-test is the simpler alternative and reads .env automatically.

Terminal 1 shows something like this:

╭─  ANOMALOUS   Critical  Critical Alert: CPU above 90% on web-01 ────────────╮
│ Detector      High CPU on web tier                                          │
│ Rule          CPU above 90%                                                 │
│ Metric        cpu.utilization                                               │
│ Source        web-01                                                        │
│ Time          2026-10-15T09:12:44+00:00                                     │
│ Incident      TEST1A2B3C4D                                                  │
│ Dimensions    env = prod                                                    │
│               host = web-01                                                 │
│ Inputs        A: 97.3  {"host": "web-01"}                                   │
│ Message       cpu.utilization has been above 90% for 5 minutes.             │
│ Runbook       https://wiki.example.com/runbooks/cpu                         │
╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

The panel is red while firing (anomalous) and green when cleared (ok / manually resolved).

Re-render stored alerts later:

sfx-olly webhook render ./data/alerts.jsonl
sfx-olly webhook render single-alert.json

docs.title: 3. Connect Splunk Observability
docs.text:
Splunk only delivers to HTTPS (TLS 1.2+) URLs reachable from the internet. Typical options:

  • A reverse proxy or ingress (nginx, Azure Application Gateway, Kubernetes ingress) that terminates TLS and forwards to the receiver.
  • WEBHOOK_SSL_CERTFILE / WEBHOOK_SSL_KEYFILE to serve TLS directly.
  • For quick experiments only: a tunnel such as ngrok http 8080.

Splunk cannot reach your laptop's localhost directly: that address refers to the machine making the request, not your laptop. For a local test, start sfx-olly webhook serve, then, in another terminal with ngrok installed and configured:

ngrok http 8080

Use the HTTPS forwarding address ngrok displays, followed by /webhooks/splunk, as the Splunk integration URL, for example https://<your-ngrok-address>/webhooks/splunk. Keep both processes running and your laptop awake; the tunnel URL may change when restarted. Only use a tunnel if your organization permits it. For production, deploy the receiver to an always-on server behind HTTPS instead of relying on your laptop.

Then, in Splunk Observability:

  1. Data Management → Add integration → Webhook → New integration
  2. URL: https://<your-host><WEBHOOK_PATH>
  3. Method: POST
  4. Shared secret: same value as WEBHOOK_SHARED_SECRET
  5. Save, then use Run test to send a test notification.
  6. Open a detector → Alert recipients → Add recipient → Webhook → your integration.

Splunk signs every request with X-SFX-Signature = base64(HMAC-SHA256(secret, body)). The receiver rejects requests without a valid signature with 401.

docs.title: End-to-end webhook test
docs.text:
Keep sfx-olly webhook serve and ngrok http 8080 running in separate terminals. If ngrok reports an unauthenticated session, sign in or create an account and run the dashboard's ngrok config add-authtoken command locally with your credential. The ngrok authtoken, WEBHOOK_SHARED_SECRET, and SFX_TOKEN are separate credentials; do not share them or commit them to source control.

  1. Local receiver: in a third terminal, run:

    bash sfx-olly webhook send-test

    Expect HTTP 200 with {"status":"accepted"} and the synthetic critical alert in the receiver terminal. This tests only local delivery.

  2. Public tunnel: replace YOUR-NGROK-HOST with the current HTTPS hostname shown by ngrok, keeping the full endpoint path:

    bash sfx-olly webhook send-test \ --url "https://YOUR-NGROK-HOST/webhooks/splunk"

    Expect HTTP 200 and another synthetic alert. This verifies the tunnel reaches the receiver, but still does not test Splunk's integration configuration.

  3. Splunk delivery: set the integration URL to that same complete HTTPS URL, set the same shared secret as the receiver, and send a test notification from Splunk. Check the receiver terminal for the notification. Ensure the integration is selected as your detector's alert recipient before expecting actual trigger/clear notifications.

If ngrok shows POST 404, open its local inspector at http://127.0.0.1:4040 and inspect the failed request's path. With the default settings it must be exactly /webhooks/splunk, not /. Also check that ngrok forwards to port 8080 and Splunk uses the current tunnel hostname. Substitute your configured path/port if different. The receiver has no POST handler at the root URL.

A 401 instead means the route was reached but signature verification failed; check that Splunk and the receiver use the same shared secret. Keep verification enabled. Do not use real secrets in screenshots or support messages; rotate any that were exposed.

docs.title: HTTP responses
docs.text: Status When 200 {"status":"accepted"} Alert accepted and dispatched to handlers 200 {"status":"duplicate"} Same incident/state/timestamp already seen within the dedupe TTL 401 Missing or invalid signature 403 Source IP not in WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_CIDRS 413 Body larger than WEBHOOK_MAX_BODY_BYTES 415 Content-Type is not application/json 422 Body is not a valid alert JSON object GET /healthz → 200 Liveness/readiness probe

docs.title: API client
docs.text:
from sfx_olly import SplunkOllyClient
from sfx_olly.exceptions import AuthenticationError, ApiError
from sfx_olly.utils import time_range, parse_duration

with SplunkOllyClient() as client:                       # reads SFX_* settings
    # metadata
    page = client.metadata.search_metrics("name:cpu.*", limit=50)
    for metric in client.metadata.iter_metrics("name:*", max_items=2_000):   # auto-pagination
        print(metric["name"])

    # raw datapoints
    start, end = time_range("1h")
    series = client.timeseries.window("sf_metric:cpu.utilization", start, end, parse_duration("5m"))

    # SignalFlow - collected results
    points = client.signalflow.execute(
        "data('cpu.utilization').mean(by=['host']).publish()", start, end
    )
    for p in points:
        print(p.timestamp_ms, p.properties.get("host"), p.value)

    # SignalFlow - raw streaming messages
    for msg in client.signalflow.stream("data('cpu.utilization').publish()", start, end):
        print(msg.event, msg.payload)

    # alerts
    detectors = client.alerts.list_detectors(name="CPU")
    incidents = client.alerts.list_incidents(include_resolved=False)

Explicit settings (for example, several orgs in one process):

from pydantic import SecretStr
from sfx_olly.config import ApiSettings
from sfx_olly import SplunkOllyClient

eu = SplunkOllyClient(ApiSettings(token=SecretStr(eu_token), realm="eu0"))
us = SplunkOllyClient(ApiSettings(token=SecretStr(us_token), realm="us1"))

Error handling:

try:
    client.metadata.get_metric("does.not.exist")
except AuthenticationError:
    ...  # 401/403
except ApiError as exc:
    print(exc.status_code, exc)

docs.title: Add a webhook handler (Slack, Teams, example telemetry, database...)
docs.text:
Any object with a handle(alert: AlertPayload) -> None method works as a handler. Handlers run after the 200 response has been sent, so a slow handler doesn't delay Splunk. If one handler fails, the error is logged and the other handlers still run.

# my_app.py
from sfx_olly.config import get_webhook_settings
from sfx_olly.webhook.app import create_app
from sfx_olly.webhook.handlers import ConsoleHandler, JsonlFileHandler
from sfx_olly.webhook.models import AlertPayload


class TeamsHandler:
    def __init__(self, url: str) -> None:
        self.url = url

    def handle(self, alert: AlertPayload) -> None:
        if alert.is_firing:
            ...  # post to Teams


settings = get_webhook_settings()
app = create_app(settings, handlers=[ConsoleHandler(), TeamsHandler("https://...")])

uvicorn my_app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080

docs.title: Add an API endpoint
docs.text:
1. Add metric methods in sfx_olly/metrics/; keep shared transport and alert APIs in sfx_olly/api/. For traces or another signal, create a separate signal package with its own API class.
  2. Use self._http.get_json(path, params) or self._http.request(...). Authentication, retries and errors are handled for you.
  3. If you created a new class, attach it in SplunkOllyClient.__init__.
  4. (Optional) Add a CLI command in sfx_olly/cli/ with a register(sub) function, then add the module to COMMAND_MODULES in cli/main.py.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Area Control Secrets Read only from env or .env. Held as SecretStr so they are never printed in reprs or config errors. Masked in every log line. Source control .env, keys, certs and alert files are listed in .gitignore. Only .env.example is committed. Transport HTTPS only (base URLs are validated). TLS verification is always on, with an optional custom CA bundle. Token leakage HTTP redirects are disabled, so the X-SF-Token header is never sent to another host. Input validation Realm checked against a pattern (blocks host injection / SSRF via realm). IDs checked against an allowlist pattern. Path segments URL-encoded. Query, program and file sizes bounded. Resilience Timeouts on every call. Bounded retries with exponential backoff that honour Retry-After. Error output API error bodies are truncated. Config errors never echo input values. Webhook auth HMAC-SHA256 signature check with constant-time comparison. A secret is mandatory by default. Webhook hardening Body size limit (streamed). Content-type check. Optional CIDR allowlist. Proxy headers trusted only from configured proxies. Replay de-duplication. Webhook surface No /docs or /openapi.json. No Server header. nosniff and no-store headers. Responses never echo the payload. Output safety Untrusted alert text has control and ANSI characters stripped and is length-limited before display. JSONL files are created with mode 0600. Defaults Binds to 127.0.0.1. Logs a warning when exposed without TLS or without signature checks.

Production recommendations:

  • Keep tokens in a secret manager (for example Azure Key Vault or Kubernetes secrets) and inject them as environment variables. Don't ship .env files to production.
  • Use a token with the least privilege you need (an API token for reads only), and rotate tokens and the webhook secret regularly.
  • Put the receiver behind TLS termination and a WAF or rate limiter.
  • Run as a non-root user.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
• API client: one pooled requests.Session per client, with pool size set by SFX_POOL_MAXSIZE. iter_metrics / iter_mts page lazily, so large result sets don't need to fit in memory. signalflow.stream() processes results as they arrive.
  • Webhook receiver: stateless and async. Alerts are handed to background tasks so Splunk gets an immediate 200. Raise WEBHOOK_WORKERS, or run several replicas behind a load balancer, and use /healthz for probes.
  • Multiple replicas: de-duplication is per process. For coordinated processing across replicas, add a handler that uses a shared store (Redis SET NX EX, or a database unique key on incidentId|state|timestamp), or publish to a durable queue and process downstream. A queue alone does not guarantee exactly-once delivery.
  • JSONL output is meant for single-host use. For multiple replicas, write to a shared sink through a custom handler.

docs.title: Dashboard has data but the filtered query is empty
docs.text:
For example, this query will be empty if the selected series do not have that literal dimension key:

sfx-olly query example.project.size --filter deployment.environment.name=env-test --range 2d

Suppose your series have environment=env-test but no deployment.environment.name dimension. These are different keys, so filtering by the missing key will not select those series. After inspecting your metric's actual dimensions, use the matching key:

sfx-olly query example.project.size --filter environment=env-test --range 2d
# compact display of the latest non-null result within that window per series:
sfx-olly query example.project.size --filter environment=env-test --range 2d --latest

These commands are fictional examples, not guaranteed data sources. --latest can return an older sample inside the window; it does not prove current availability. Compare the dashboard's actual SignalFlow, filters, time window, resolution, rollup, and realm/org if differences remain. To investigate your metric:

sfx-olly metrics inspect example.project.size
sfx-olly mts search 'sf_metric:example.project.size AND environment:env-test'
sfx-olly query example.project.size --range 2d --latest
sfx-olly query example.project.size --filter environment=env-test --range 2d --dry-run
sfx-olly -v query example.project.size --filter environment=env-test --range 2d --latest

Do not guess aliases between env, environment, and deployment.environment.name. Sparse metrics may need a wider range; match the dashboard rather than inventing data with extrapolation. Aborted SignalFlow computations now raise errors instead of appearing empty.

Symptom Fix HTTP 400 ... Unsupported query syntax Search endpoints need field:value syntax. Bare terms are now prefixed automatically. To get metric values, use sfx-olly query <metric>. Configuration error ... token: Field required Set SFX_TOKEN in .env or the environment. HTTP 401/403 The token is invalid, expired, or an ingest-only token. Use an API-scoped token. invalid realm Use your org realm from Settings → Organization (e.g. eu0). SSL errors behind a corporate proxy Set SFX_CA_BUNDLE to the proxy CA file. WEBHOOK_SHARED_SECRET is required Set the secret, or set WEBHOOK_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE=false for local tests only. Webhook returns 401 The secret in Splunk and WEBHOOK_SHARED_SECRET don't match. Webhook returns 403 The caller IP isn't in WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_CIDRS. Behind a proxy, set WEBHOOK_TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true and WEBHOOK_FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS. Need request details Set LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG. Tokens stay redacted.
